claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Loss of function of KIF1A in mice leads to sensorimotor deficits and early postnatal death.
claims.source: In mice, loss of function of unc-104's mammalian homologue, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995), leads to the accumulation of SVPs in the cell body and a dramatic reduction in the number of SVs at synapses, along with sensorimotor deficits and early postnatal death (Yonekawa et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: HTT plays a prominent role in axonal transport.
claims.source: Mice bearing mutations in Huntingtin (HTT), a protein that plays a prominent role in axonal transport (Saudou and Humbert, 2016), provide one model system that could illuminate the role of SVP transport on synaptic homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: HTT scaffolds various cargoes including endosomes, autophagosomes, and vesicles containing BDNF and APP.
claims.source: HTT scaffolds various cargoes—endosomes, autophagosomes, vesicles containing BDNF, APP, etc. (Bruyère et al., 2020; Cason et al., 2021; Caviston et al., 2011; Fu and Holzbaur, 2014; Gauthier et al., 2004; Her and Goldstein, 2008; Liot et al., 2013; Wong and Holzbaur, 2014)—along with the appropriate molecular motors for anterograde or retrograde transport and any adaptor proteins that may be needed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The direction of HTT-mediated transport is dictated by its phosphorylation at serine 421.
claims.source: Because the direction of HTT-mediated transport is dictated by its phosphorylation at serine 421 (Bruyère et al., 2020; Colin et al., 2008; Ehinger et al., 2020; Vitet et al., 2020), we were able to investigate how mutations at this site affect axonal transport of SVPs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles.
claims.source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the number of anterograde VAMP2-positive vesicles.
claims.source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the linear flow rate of VAMP2-positive vesicles.
claims.source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse.
claims.source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: There was no significant effect of HTT-SA mutation on VAMP2-mCherry vesicle velocities or net directional flux in axons.
claims.source: There was no significant effect on VAMP2-mCherry vesicle velocities or net directional flux of HTT-SA mutation in axons (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The frequency of VGLUT1-pHluorin release events at synapses was significantly greater in HTT-SD neurons.
claims.source: The amplitude of VGLUT1 events was similar in WT, HTT-SA, and HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but the frequency of release events at synapses was significantly greater only in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The amplitude of VGLUT1 events was similar in WT, HTT-SA, and HTT-SD neurons.
claims.source: The amplitude of VGLUT1 events was similar in WT, HTT-SA, and HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but the frequency of release events at synapses was significantly greater only in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: HTT-SD and HTT-SA mice showed no differences from WT in motor coordination.
claims.source: We had previously characterized HTT-SA, HTT-SD, and WT mice and found no differences between them in motor coordination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), forelimb strength (grip test), or anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test) (Ehinger et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous experimental data cited from Ehinger et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: HTT-SD and HTT-SA mice showed no differences from WT in forelimb strength (grip test).
claims.source: We had previously characterized HTT-SA, HTT-SD, and WT mice and found no differences between them in motor coordination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), forelimb strength (grip test), or anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test) (Ehinger et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous experimental data cited from Ehinger et al., 2020.

claims.claim: HTT-SD and HTT-SA mice showed no differences from WT in anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test).
claims.source: We had previously characterized HTT-SA, HTT-SD, and WT mice and found no differences between them in motor coordination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), forelimb strength (grip test), or anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test) (Ehinger et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous experimental data cited from Ehinger et al., 2020.

claims.claim: WT mice nearly doubled their latency to fall over the first 3 days/30 sessions of rotarod training.
claims.source: Over the 8 days, the WT mice nearly doubled their latency to fall over the first 3 days/30 sessions of training (the learning phase) and then maintained that skill (the consolidation phase) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: HTT-SD mice did not improve as much as WT during the initial learning phase of rotarod training and plateaued at a lower level of skill.
claims.source: The HTT-SD mice did not improve as much during the initial learning phase and plateaued at a lower level of skill.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: HTT-SA mice learned more gradually than WT on the rotarod but by the eighth day were virtually equivalent.
claims.source: The HTT-SA mice learned much more gradually than WT but by the eighth day were virtually equivalent.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Motor skill learning relies on communication between the dorsal striatum and layer V pyramidal neurons in the motor cortex via the release of glutamate by the cortical afferences.
claims.source: Motor skill learning relies on communication between the dorsal striatum and layer V pyramidal neurons in the motor cortex via the release of glutamate by the cortical afferences (Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Jin and Costa, 2015; Perrin and Venance, 2019; Yin and Knowlton, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: HTT-SD mice did not differ from WT or HTT-SA mice in sEPSC amplitude or frequency.
claims.source: The HTT-SD mice did not differ from WT or HTT-SA mice in sEPSC amplitude or frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In WT mice, corticostriatal short-term plasticity was facilitated for short ISIs (25 and 50 ms), with a lack of significant plasticity at 100 ms followed by a short-term depression for longer ISIs (250 and 500 ms).
claims.source: Paired-pulse ratio (PPR) analysis revealed that in WT mice, corticostriatal short-term plasticity was facilitated for short ISIs (25 and 50 ms), with a lack of significant plasticity at 100 ms followed by a short-term depression for longer ISIs (250 and 500 ms), as previously described (Goubard et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: In HTT-SD mice, there was no short-term facilitation but only depression starting from 100 ms ISIs.
claims.source: In HTT-SD mice, there was no short-term facilitation but only depression starting from 100 ms ISIs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: HTT-SA mice showed a short-term plasticity similar to WT mice, except that the facilitation expression window widened up to 100 ms ISIs.
claims.source: HTT-SA mice showed a short-term plasticity similar to WT mice, except that the facilitation expression window widened up to 100 ms ISIs (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The lower facilitation in HTT-SD MSNs indicates that constitutive phosphorylation of HTT increases the probability of glutamate release in pyramidal cells.
claims.source: The lower facilitation in HTT-SD MSNs indicates that constitutive phosphorylation of HTT increases the probability of glutamate release in pyramidal cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data showing altered short-term plasticity.

claims.claim: Decreased facilitation could indicate changes in the number of SVs at the presynapse.
claims.source: Since decreased facilitation could indicate changes in the number of SVs at the presynapse (Park et al., 2012; Pulido and Marty, 2017), we investigated the number of SVs at axon terminals within the corticostriatal network using electron microscopy.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), the number of synapses did not change.
claims.source: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), the number of synapses did not change (Figure 4Bi) but there were a greater number of SVs at the axon terminals than in WT mice (Figure 4Bii).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Bi.

claims.claim: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), there were a greater number of SVs at the axon terminals than in WT mice.
claims.source: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), the number of synapses did not change (Figure 4Bi) but there were a greater number of SVs at the axon terminals than in WT mice (Figure 4Bii).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Bii.

claims.claim: The presynaptic size was smaller in the HTT-SD corticostriatal synapses.
claims.source: The presynaptic size was smaller in the HTT-SD corticostriatal synapses (Figure 4Biii), leading to an increase in SV density in HTT-SD presynaptic terminals (Figure 4Biv).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Biii.

claims.claim: HTT-SD presynaptic terminals have an increased SV density.
claims.source: The presynaptic size was smaller in the HTT-SD corticostriatal synapses (Figure 4Biii), leading to an increase in SV density in HTT-SD presynaptic terminals (Figure 4Biv).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Biv.

claims.claim: HTT-SD axon terminals exhibited a greater density of SVs in the most distal zone (zone 3).
claims.source: There was no difference between the genotypes in terms of the area of the zones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), but HTT-SD axon terminals exhibited a greater density of SVs in the most distal zone (zone 3) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: HTT-SA axon terminals had fewer vesicles than WT.
claims.source: The fact that HTT-SA axon terminals had fewer vesicles lends further support to this explanation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: KIF1A is in the proteome of HTT-associated vesicles.
claims.source: We observed KIF1A in the proteome of HTT-associated vesicles (Figure 5A; Migazzi et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A and cited from Migazzi et al., 2021.

claims.claim: KIF1A colocalizes with HTT immunopositive puncta in free-cultured cortical neurons at DIV 5.
claims.source: We found that KIF1A colocalizes with HTT immunopositive puncta in free-cultured cortical neurons at DIV 5 using a two-dimensional stimulated emission depletion (2D-STED) super-resolution microscope (Figure 5B, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 2D-STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There is greater colocalization of HTT with KIF1A and VAMP2 in HTT-SD neuronal circuits than in WT.
claims.source: We assessed this possibility by permeabilizing isolated axons within the distal part of microfluidic axonal compartments and, using Airyscan confocal high-resolution microscopy, we observed greater colocalization of HTT with KIF1A and VAMP2 in HTT-SD neuronal circuits than in WT (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Airyscan microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: There is a significantly greater PLA signal for HTT-KIF1A interaction in HTT-SD neurons.
claims.source: We then used proximity ligation assay (PLA) to confirm the in cellulo interaction between HTT and KIF1A. We observed a significantly greater PLA signal in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 5D), despite no change in PLA levels of VAMP2 with HTT and KIF1A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: HTT-SD showed a greater vesicular/cytosolic ratio for KIF1A.
claims.source: Finally, we prepared vesicular-enriched fractions from WT and HTT-SD mouse brains and immunoblotted them for KIF1A. HTT-SD showed a greater vesicular/cytosolic ratio for KIF1A (Figure 5E), while p150 remained constant and the total brain levels of KIF1A did not differ between the genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The total brain levels of KIF1A did not differ between WT and HTT-SD genotypes.
claims.source: Finally, we prepared vesicular-enriched fractions from WT and HTT-SD mouse brains and immunoblotted them for KIF1A. HTT-SD showed a greater vesicular/cytosolic ratio for KIF1A (Figure 5E), while p150 remained constant and the total brain levels of KIF1A did not differ between the genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Silencing KIF1A in WT cortical neurons decreased VAMP2 anterograde vesicle velocity.
claims.source: We found that silencing KIF1A in WT cortical neurons decreased VAMP2 anterograde vesicle velocity, the number of anterograde vesicles (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), the linear flow (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), and the net directional flux of VAMP2 vesicles toward the axon terminals (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Silencing KIF1A in HTT-SD reduced the anterograde velocity of VAMP2 vesicles close to values observed in WT neurons.
claims.source: Silencing KIF1A in HTT-SD reduced the anterograde velocity of VAMP2 vesicles close to values observed in WT neurons (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: KIF1A silencing reduced the number of anterograde vesicles, linear flow, and net directional flux in HTT-SD to values found in WT.
claims.source: KIF1A silencing also reduced the number of anterograde vesicles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), linear flow, and net directional flux in HTT-SD to values found in WT (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The velocity and number of retrograde-moving VAMP2 vesicles was lower in HTT-SD neurons after KIF1A silencing.
claims.source: The velocity and number of retrograde-moving VAMP2 vesicles was also lower in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: KIF1A has a reported role as a dynein activator.
claims.source: This attenuation of retrograde transport might be linked to KIF1A's reported role as a dynein activator (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Chronic HTT phosphorylation increased the anterograde transport, the linear flow, and the net directional flux of BDNF-containing vesicles.
claims.source: Chronic HTT phosphorylation increased the anterograde transport, the linear flow, and the net directional flux of BDNF-containing vesicles, in agreement with previous studies (Colin et al., 2008; Ehinger et al., 2020; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Silencing KIF1A did not affect BDNF dynamics either in WT or in HTT-SD neurons.
claims.source: Silencing KIF1A did not affect BDNF dynamics either in WT or in HTT-SD neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The phospho-HTT-dependent increase in SVP anterograde transport, in contrast to BDNF, is mediated by KIF1A.
claims.source: This indicates that the phospho-HTT-dependent increase in SVP anterograde transport, in contrast to BDNF, is mediated by KIF1A.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of KIF1A silencing on VAMP2 vs. BDNF transport.

claims.claim: WT sh-Kif1a presynapses showed significantly fewer SVs than WT sh-Scr presynapses.
claims.source: WT sh-Kif1a presynapses showed significantly fewer SVs than WT sh-Scr presynapses (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The number of SVs at presynapses in HTT-SD brains treated with sh-Kif1a reverted to WT levels.
claims.source: As previously shown (Figure 4B), there were significantly more SVs at presynapses in HTT-SD, but this number reverted to WT levels in HTT-SD brains treated with sh-Kif1a (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Decreasing the phospho-HTT-mediated anterograde transport of SVPs by reducing KIF1A levels in corticostriatal-projecting neurons reduces the number of SVs at presynapses.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that decreasing the phospho-HTT-mediated anterograde transport of SVPs by reducing KIF1A levels in corticostriatal-projecting neurons reduces the number of SVs at presynapses.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that sh-Kif1a treatment reduces SV numbers.

claims.claim: There is a close relationship between axonal transport and synaptic SV content.
claims.source: This in turn indicates a close relationship between axonal transport and synaptic SV content.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that manipulating axonal transport affects SV numbers at synapses.

claims.claim: Silencing KIF1A improved the performance of HTT-SD mice on the rotarod over the first 6 days.
claims.source: HTT-SD mice did not show much improvement over 8 days (Figure 8B), as with the non-injected mice (Figure 2B). Silencing KIF1A improved the performance of the HTT-SD mice over the first 6 days, but then the mice seemed to lose ground (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The improvement in motor learning of the HTT-SD mice via sh-Kif1a silencing was significant on the first day of training, but the effect did not last until the eighth day.
claims.source: Indeed, the improvement in motor learning of the HTT-SD mice via sh-Kif1a silencing was significant on the first day of training, but the effect did not last until the eighth day (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons influences the number of SVs at synapses.
claims.source: Nonetheless, these findings indicate that HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons, a process modulated by phosphorylation, influences the number of SVs at synapses, the probability of release, and the efficacy of motor skill learning.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing that manipulating the HTT-KIF1A pathway affects SV numbers.

claims.claim: HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons influences the probability of release.
claims.source: Nonetheless, these findings indicate that HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons, a process modulated by phosphorylation, influences the number of SVs at synapses, the probability of release, and the efficacy of motor skill learning.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing that manipulating the HTT-KIF1A pathway affects short-term plasticity.

claims.claim: HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons influences the efficacy of motor skill learning.
claims.source: Nonetheless, these findings indicate that HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons, a process modulated by phosphorylation, influences the number of SVs at synapses, the probability of release, and the efficacy of motor skill learning.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing that manipulating the HTT-KIF1A pathway affects rotarod performance.

claims.claim: The anterograde transport of SVP is driven predominantly by the kinesin-3 motor KIF1A.
claims.source: The anterograde transport of SVP is driven predominantly by the kinesin-3 motor KIF1A (Guedes-Dias and Holzbaur, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: HTT and KIF1A interactomes suggested a possible interaction between the two proteins.
claims.source: HTT and KIF1A interactomes suggested a possible interaction between the two proteins (Shirasaki et al., 2012; Stucchi et al., 2018), but this had not been tested.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Axonal transport of SVPs influences synaptic function.
claims.source: We show here that axonal transport of SVPs influences synaptic function.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: HTT's phosphorylation status fine-tunes SVP transport efficiency through its recruitment of KIF1A.
claims.source: Specifically, HTT's phosphorylation status fine-tunes SVP transport efficiency through its recruitment of KIF1A.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that HTT phosphorylation affects KIF1A recruitment and SVP transport.

claims.claim: Genetically blocking dephosphorylation at S421 impaired motor learning.
claims.source: Genetically blocking dephosphorylation at S421 impaired motor learning, and abolishing KIF1A activity in the context of constitutive phosphorylation only partially restored motor performance on the rotarod.
claims.evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data from HTT-SD mice.

claims.claim: Abolishing KIF1A activity in the context of constitutive phosphorylation only partially restored motor performance on the rotarod.
claims.source: Genetically blocking dephosphorylation at S421 impaired motor learning, and abolishing KIF1A activity in the context of constitutive phosphorylation only partially restored motor performance on the rotarod.
claims.evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data from HTT-SD mice treated with sh-Kif1a.

claims.claim: DENN/MADD, a Rab3-GEP that binds to KIF1A (and KIF1Bß), regulates SVP binding to microtubules according to Rab3's nucleotide state.
claims.source: This work places HTT among the proteins that participate in SVP transport (Guedes-Dias and Holzbaur, 2019) and closes a loop opened by the discovery that DENN/MADD, a Rab3-GEP that binds to KIF1A (and KIF1Bß), regulates SVP binding to microtubules according to Rab3's nucleotide state (Niwa et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome.
claims.source: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome (Shirasaki et al., 2012) and enriched in SVs (Takamori et al., 2006); previous work in Drosophila larval axons showed that reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles (White et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Rab3 is enriched in SVs.
claims.source: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome (Shirasaki et al., 2012) and enriched in SVs (Takamori et al., 2006); previous work in Drosophila larval axons showed that reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles (White et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles in Drosophila larval axons.
claims.source: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome (Shirasaki et al., 2012) and enriched in SVs (Takamori et al., 2006); previous work in Drosophila larval axons showed that reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles (White et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: In the context of Huntington disease (HD), both Rab3 levels and the conversion from GTP to GDP state are dysregulated.
claims.source: In the context of Huntington disease (HD), which is caused by polyglutamine expansions in HTT, both Rab3 levels and the conversion from GTP to GDP state are dysregulated, which is consistent with a role for HTT in the transport of SVPs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact about HD pathology.

claims.claim: Studies in HD models have revealed alterations in HTT phosphorylation at S421 that could result from defects in Akt, the S421 kinase, or dysregulation of the phosphatases calcineurin (PP2B) and PP2A.
claims.source: Studies in HD models have revealed alterations in HTT phosphorylation at S421 that could result from defects in Akt, the S421 kinase, or dysregulation of the phosphatases calcineurin (PP2B) and PP2A (Humbert et al., 2002; Metzler et al., 2010; Pardo et al., 2006; Warby et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Promoting HTT phosphorylation is neuroprotective, as it restores the transport and release of BDNF.
claims.source: That such a study would be worthwhile is suggested by the fact that promoting HTT phosphorylation is neuroprotective, as it restores the transport and release of BDNF (Humbert et al., 2002; Kratter et al., 2016; Pardo et al., 2006; Pineda et al., 2009; Warby et al., 2009; Zala et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips.
claims.source: It is interesting to note in this context that release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips (Virlogeux et al., 2018) and in vivo (Fernández-García et al., 2020; Smith-Dijak et al., 2019) and that stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice (Fernández-García et al., 2020), suggesting that reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in vivo in HD.
claims.source: It is interesting to note in this context that release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips (Virlogeux et al., 2018) and in vivo (Fernández-García et al., 2020; Smith-Dijak et al., 2019) and that stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice (Fernández-García et al., 2020), suggesting that reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice.
claims.source: It is interesting to note in this context that release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips (Virlogeux et al., 2018) and in vivo (Fernández-García et al., 2020; Smith-Dijak et al., 2019) and that stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice (Fernández-García et al., 2020), suggesting that reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential in HD.
claims.source: It is interesting to note in this context that release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips (Virlogeux et al., 2018) and in vivo (Fernández-García et al., 2020; Smith-Dijak et al., 2019) and that stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice (Fernández-García et al., 2020), suggesting that reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the cited research.

claims.claim: Genetically impairing KIF1A reduces the number of SVs at nerve terminals and causes postnatal lethality.
claims.source: Indeed, genetically impairing KIF1A reduces the number of SVs at nerve terminals and causes postnatal lethality (Yonekawa et al., 1998).

claims.claim: KIF1A loss-of-function variants are associated with four diseases: autosomal recessive hereditary sensory neuropathy IIC, autosomal dominant mental retardation (ADMR) type 9, autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 30, and autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP).

results.result: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD) increases axonal transport of synaptic vesicle precursors (SVPs) and enhances synaptic glutamate release. In microfluidic devices, HTT-SD neurons showed increased anterograde velocity, number, linear flow rate, and net directional flux of VAMP2-positive vesicles compared to WT, while HTT-SA showed no significant differences. HTT-SD neurons also exhibited significantly greater frequency of VGLUT1-pHluorin release events at synapses, though event amplitude remained unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C27-C33 are well-supported by converging experimental evidence from microfluidic devices. The data show consistent increases in multiple transport parameters (velocity, number, flow rate, flux) for VAMP2 vesicles in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1B and supplements), and increased glutamate release frequency measured by VGLUT1-pHluorin exocytosis (Figure 1C). The lack of effect in HTT-SA provides an important control demonstrating specificity to phosphorylation.

results.result: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation impairs motor skill learning in mice. HTT-SD mice showed impaired learning on the rotarod task over 8 days, improving less during the initial learning phase and plateauing at lower skill levels compared to WT. HTT-SA mice learned more gradually but eventually reached WT-equivalent performance by day 8.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C37-C39, C81 are supported by behavioral data from rotarod experiments (Figure 2B-D). The HTT-SD phenotype is consistent across multiple days of training with appropriate statistical analysis. The HTT-SA phenotype is milder and shows eventual recovery, providing a useful comparison. Sample sizes appear adequate (N=20 WT vs 20 HTT-SD, 13 WT vs 18 HTT-SA) and the behavioral paradigm is well-established.

results.result: HTT phosphorylation alters short-term synaptic plasticity at corticostriatal synapses. HTT-SD mice showed loss of short-term facilitation and only depression starting at 100ms ISIs, while WT mice showed facilitation at short ISIs (25-50ms) followed by depression at longer ISIs. HTT-SA mice showed similar plasticity to WT but with a widened facilitation window extending to 100ms ISIs. This indicates increased probability of glutamate release in HTT-SD pyramidal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by paired-pulse ratio electrophysiology data (Figure 3). The loss of facilitation in HTT-SD is a robust finding consistent with increased release probability. Sample sizes are adequate (N=13 WT, 12 HTT-SD, 12 HTT-SA MSNs from ≥3 mice). The interpretation linking decreased facilitation to increased release probability is well-established in the field and supported by citations. The sEPSC data (C41) provides an important control showing no baseline differences.

results.result: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation increases synaptic vesicle number and density at corticostriatal synapses. Electron microscopy revealed that HTT-SD mice had more SVs at axon terminals than WT, with smaller presynaptic size leading to increased SV density. The increase was particularly pronounced in the most distal zone (zone 3) from the active zone. HTT-SA mice showed fewer vesicles than WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are well-supported by quantitative electron microscopy data (Figure 4). The analysis is rigorous with large sample sizes (N=279 WT and 171 HTT-SD terminals from multiple mice) and appropriate statistical tests. The spatial analysis dividing the presynapse into zones provides mechanistic insight. The HTT-SA data (C52) provides an important bidirectional control. The finding that synapse number is unchanged (C47) is an important control ruling out developmental effects.

results.result: HTT recruits KIF1A to vesicles, and this interaction is enhanced by HTT phosphorylation. KIF1A was identified in the proteome of HTT-associated vesicles and colocalizes with HTT in neurons. HTT-SD showed greater colocalization of HTT with KIF1A and VAMP2, increased PLA signal for HTT-KIF1A interaction, and higher vesicular/cytosolic ratio of KIF1A, while total KIF1A levels remained unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58, C78 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: mass spectrometry (C53), super-resolution microscopy (C54), Airyscan microscopy (C55), proximity ligation assay (C56), and biochemical fractionation (C57-C58). The convergence of evidence from different techniques strengthens the conclusion. The finding that total KIF1A levels are unchanged (C58) is an important control showing the effect is due to redistribution rather than expression changes.

results.result: The phospho-HTT-dependent increase in SVP transport is mediated by KIF1A. Silencing KIF1A in WT neurons decreased VAMP2 vesicle transport parameters, while silencing KIF1A in HTT-SD neurons restored transport to WT levels. In contrast, KIF1A silencing did not affect BDNF transport in either WT or HTT-SD neurons, demonstrating cargo specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63, C67 are well-supported by KIF1A knockdown experiments in microfluidic devices (Figure 6). The sh-Kif1a achieved ~83% knockdown (Figure 6—supplement 1A). The rescue of HTT-SD transport phenotype by KIF1A silencing provides strong evidence for mechanism. The BDNF control experiments (C65-C67) are critical for demonstrating specificity and ruling out general transport defects. Sample sizes appear adequate across multiple independent experiments.

results.result: Reducing KIF1A levels in corticostriatal-projecting neurons normalizes synaptic vesicle numbers in HTT-SD mice. Stereotaxic injection of sh-Kif1a into motor cortex reduced SV numbers at WT presynapses and restored the elevated SV numbers in HTT-SD presynapses to WT levels, demonstrating a direct relationship between axonal transport and synaptic SV content.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by in vivo electron microscopy following stereotaxic lentiviral injections (Figure 7). The experimental design appropriately targets corticostriatal projections, and the EM analysis is quantitative with adequate sample sizes (N=360 WT sh-Scr, 324 WT sh-Kif1a, 417 HTT-SD sh-Scr, 337 HTT-SD sh-Kif1a synapses from 3 mice per condition). The bidirectional effects (reduction in WT, normalization in HTT-SD) strengthen the causal interpretation.

results.result: Silencing KIF1A in motor cortex partially rescues motor learning deficits in HTT-SD mice. KIF1A knockdown improved rotarod performance in HTT-SD mice during the first 6 days of training, with significant improvement on day 1, but the effect did not persist through day 8.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C72-C73, C82 are supported by in vivo behavioral experiments following stereotaxic injections (Figure 8). The partial rescue during early learning but not late consolidation is clearly documented. Sample sizes are adequate (N=12 WT sh-Scr, 11 WT sh-Kif1a, 10 HTT-SD sh-Scr, 12 HTT-SD sh-Kif1a mice). The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation that the effect is transient and discuss potential explanations (duration of gene silencing, circuit consolidation). The partial nature of the rescue is important for understanding the complexity of the phenotype.

results.result: HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs influences synaptic plasticity and motor skill learning. The authors conclude that HTT phosphorylation fine-tunes SVP transport efficiency through KIF1A recruitment, affecting SV numbers at synapses, release probability, and motor learning efficacy in the corticostriatal network.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C74-C76, C79-C80 represent the main integrative conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergence of evidence from multiple experimental systems (microfluidics, brain slices, in vivo mice) and multiple techniques (imaging, electrophysiology, EM, behavior). The mechanistic chain from HTT phosphorylation → KIF1A recruitment → SVP transport → SV accumulation → altered release probability → impaired learning is documented at each step with appropriate controls.

results.result: HTT-SD and HTT-SA mice show no baseline differences from WT in motor coordination, forelimb strength, or anxious-depressive behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are important negative controls supported by previous characterization (Ehinger et al., 2020) and confirmed for motor coordination in Figure 2—supplement 1A. These controls are essential for establishing that the rotarod learning deficits are specific to motor skill learning rather than general motor or behavioral impairments. The citation to prior work is appropriate for grip test and elevated plus maze data.

results.result: HTT-SD mice show no differences in spontaneous EPSC amplitude or frequency compared to WT or HTT-SA mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C41 is an important negative control supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 3—supplement 1). This demonstrates that the changes in short-term plasticity are not due to baseline differences in synaptic transmission or excitability, strengthening the interpretation that the effects are specific to activity-dependent release probability.

results.result: Background on synaptic vesicle biology and the prevailing view that axonal transport does not affect synaptic function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C12-C16 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims set up the conceptual framework and prior assumptions that the study challenges. The citations are to authoritative reviews and primary research.

results.result: Prior work in model organisms and mice has linked severe disruptions in SVP transport to synaptic and behavioral deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C26 summarize relevant prior work in C. elegans, Drosophila, and mice, all supported by appropriate citations. This background establishes that complete loss of transport motors causes severe phenotypes, motivating the study of more subtle modulation. The citations appear accurate and relevant.

results.result: Background on motor learning circuits, KIF1A function, and connections to HTT and Rab3.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C77, C83-C86 provide relevant background on corticostriatal circuits, KIF1A as the primary SVP motor, and connections to HTT and Rab3 signaling. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. This background contextualizes the experimental findings within established knowledge.

results.result: Discussion of relevance to Huntington's disease and potential therapeutic implications.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 discuss implications for Huntington's disease. While C87-C92 are supported by citations to prior work, C93 is explicitly speculative about therapeutic potential. The connection to HD is reasonable given that the study uses HTT mutants, but the therapeutic implications are not directly tested. The authors appropriately frame this as speculation ('could have therapeutic potential').

results.result: Discussion of human diseases associated with KIF1A mutations and the importance of balanced SVP transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 discuss human genetic diseases associated with KIF1A mutations, all supported by appropriate citations. This discussion contextualizes the findings within human disease and emphasizes that both too little and too much SVP transport can be pathological, which is consistent with the experimental findings.

results.result: Discussion of synaptic vesicle pool organization and dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C108 discuss the organization of SV pools (RRP, recycling pool, reserve pool) and their dynamics, all supported by appropriate citations. C105 is explicitly framed as a proposal ('we propose') based on the authors' data and prior work. This discussion provides important context for interpreting the EM findings showing increased SVs in the distal zone.

results.result: Discussion of the roles of dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum in motor learning and consolidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 discuss the roles of different striatal regions in motor learning, supported by multiple citations. This discussion addresses why targeting DLS might rescue early learning but not late consolidation, providing a plausible explanation for the partial rescue observed with KIF1A knockdown.

results.result: KIF1A has a reported role as a dynein activator, and chronic HTT phosphorylation increases BDNF transport while KIF1A silencing does not affect BDNF dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by experimental data (Figure 6—supplement 2B) and citations. The BDNF control experiments are important for demonstrating cargo specificity. The observation that KIF1A silencing affects retrograde VAMP2 transport (C63) is discussed in relation to KIF1A's role as a dynein activator (C64), providing a mechanistic interpretation.
